3: The breath was from my lungs so milked away, When I was up, that I could go no farther, Nay, I sat down upon my first arrival.
8: “Now it behoves thee thus to put off sloth,” My Master said; “for sitting upon down, Or under quilt, one cometh not to fame,
12: Withouten which whoso his life consumes Such vestige leaveth of himself on earth, As smoke in air or in the water foam.
16: And therefore raise thee up, o’ercome the anguish With spirit that o’ercometh every battle, If with its heavy body it sink not.
20: A longer stairway it behoves thee mount; ’Tis not enough from these to have departed; Let it avail thee, if thou understand me.”
24: Then I uprose, showing myself provided Better with breath than I did feel myself, And said: “Go on, for I am strong and bold.”
29: Upward we took our way along the crag, Which jagged was, and narrow, and difficult, And more precipitous far than that before.
33: Speaking I went, not to appear exhausted; Whereat a voice from the next moat came forth, Not well adapted to articulate words.
38: I know not what it said, though o’er the back I now was of the arch that passes there; But he seemed moved to anger who was speaking.
43: I was bent downward, but my living eyes Could not attain the bottom, for the dark; Wherefore I: “Master, see that thou arrive
47: At the next round, and let us descend the wall; For as from hence I hear and understand not, So I look down and nothing I distinguish.”
52: “Other response,” he said, “I make thee not, Except the doing; for the modest asking Ought to be followed by the deed in silence.”
57: We from the bridge descended at its head, Where it connects itself with the eighth bank, And then was manifest to me the Bolgia;
61: And I beheld therein a terrible throng Of serpents, and of such a monstrous kind, That the remembrance still congeals my blood
65: Let Libya boast no longer with her sand; For if Chelydri, Jaculi, and Phareae She breeds, with Cenchri and with Amphisbaena,
70: Neither so many plagues nor so malignant E’er showed she with all Ethiopia, Nor with whatever on the Red Sea is!
74: Among this cruel and most dismal throng People were running naked and affrighted. Without the hope of hole or heliotrope.
79: They had their hands with serpents bound behind them; These riveted upon their reins the tail And head, and were in front of them entwined.
84: And lo! at one who was upon our side There darted forth a serpent, which transfixed him There where the neck is knotted to the shoulders.
88: Nor ‘O’ so quickly e’er, nor ‘I’ was written, As he took fire, and burned; and ashes wholly Behoved it that in falling he became.
93: And when he on the ground was thus destroyed, The ashes drew together, and of themselves Into himself they instantly returned.
98: Even thus by the great sages ’tis confessed The phoenix dies, and then is born again, When it approaches its five-hundredth year;
103: On herb or grain it feeds not in its life, But only on tears of incense and amomum, And nard and myrrh are its last winding-sheet.
108: And as he is who falls, and knows not how, By force of demons who to earth down drag him, Or other oppilation that binds man,
113: When he arises and around him looks, Wholly bewildered by the mighty anguish Which he has suffered, and in looking sighs;
118: Such was that sinner after he had risen. Justice of God! O how severe it is, That blows like these in vengeance poureth down!
123: The Guide thereafter asked him who he was; Whence he replied: “I rained from Tuscany A short time since into this cruel gorge.
127: A bestial life, and not a human, pleased me, Even as the mule I was; I’m Vanni Fucci, Beast, and Pistoia was my worthy den.”
131: And I unto the Guide: “Tell him to stir not, And ask what crime has thrust him here below, For once a man of blood and wrath I saw him.”
136: And the sinner, who had heard, dissembled not, But unto me directed mind and face, And with a melancholy shame was painted.
141: Then said: “It pains me more that thou hast caught me Amid this misery where thou seest me, Than when I from the other life was taken.
146: What thou demandest I cannot deny; So low am I put down because I robbed The sacristy of the fair ornaments,
150: And falsely once ’twas laid upon another; But that thou mayst not such a sight enjoy, If thou shalt e’er be out of the dark places,
155:
Thine ears to my announcement ope and hear: Pistoia first of Neri groweth meagre; Then Florence doth renew her men and manners;

Mars draws a vapour up from Val di Magra, Which is with turbid clouds enveloped round, And with impetuous and bitter tempest
156: Over Campo Picen shall be the battle; When it shall suddenly rend the mist asunder, So that each Bianco shall thereby be smitten.
159: And this I’ve said that it may give thee pain.”
161: At the conclusion of his words, the thief Lifted his hands aloft with both the figs, Crying: “Take that, God, for at thee I aim them.”
163: From that time forth the serpents were my friends; For one entwined itself about his neck As if it said: “I will not thou speak more;”
164: And round his arms another, and rebound him, Clinching itself together so in front, That with them he could not a motion make.
165:
Pistoia, ah, Pistoia! why resolve not To burn thyself to ashes and so perish, Since in ill-doing thou thy seed excellest?

Through all the sombre circles of this Hell, Spirit I saw not against God so proud, Not he who fell at Thebes down from the walls!
166: He fled away, and spake no further word; And I beheld a Centaur full of rage Come crying out: “Where is, where is the scoffer?”
167:
I do not think Maremma has so many Serpents as he had all along his back, As far as where our countenance begins.

Upon the shoulders, just behind the nape, With wings wide open was a dragon lying, And he sets fire to all that he encounters.

My Master said: “That one is Cacus, who Beneath the rock upon Mount Aventine Created oftentimes a lake of blood.
169: He goes not on the same road with his brothers, By reason of the fraudulent theft he made Of the great herd, which he had near to him;
170: Whereat his tortuous actions ceased beneath The mace of Hercules, who peradventure Gave him a hundred, and he felt not ten.”
171:
While he was speaking thus, he had passed by, And spirits three had underneath us come, Of which nor I aware was, nor my Leader,

Until what time they shouted: “Who are you?” On which account our story made a halt, And then we were intent on them alone.
172: I did not know them; but it came to pass, As it is wont to happen by some chance, That one to name the other was compelled,
174:
Exclaiming: “Where can Cianfa have remained?” Whence I, so that the Leader might attend, Upward from chin to nose my finger laid.

If thou art, Reader, slow now to believe What I shall say, it will no marvel be, For I who saw it hardly can admit it.
175:
As I was holding raised on them my brows, Behold! a serpent with six feet darts forth In front of one, and fastens wholly on him.

With middle feet it bound him round the paunch, And with the forward ones his arms it seized; Then thrust its teeth through one cheek and the other;
